k-accomplished.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>sheep</radical> is being driven up a track: the <radical>road</radical> sweeps in underneath it, the surface <radical>splits</radical> into ruts, and packed <radical>earth</radical> climbs the whole way up. It is a long haul and the flock keeps stopping dead. But the last one is over the top and into the pen, and the job is <radical>accomplished</radical>.
k-accomplished.reading_mnemonic: Tatsu is the drover who marks the top of every hill the same way: one slap on the gatepost and a barked 「<reading>たつ</reading>」 — done, next. He has said it at every gate between here and the coast. たつ means it is finished.

k-ancestor.meaning_mnemonic: An <radical>altar</radical> stands on the left, and stacked on the right is an <radical>eye</radical> laid flat above a line of <radical>ground</radical> — a portrait propped up over the offerings, watching the room. Somebody long dead is looking back at you off that shelf. You bow to the face because it is your <radical>ancestor</radical>.
k-ancestor.reading_mnemonic: So is the small catch of sound the incense makes when it takes light at the altar — 「<reading>そ</reading>」 — and for a second the eye in the portrait seems to move. One syllable, once a year, for the ancestor. そ.

k-breath.meaning_mnemonic: Your own <radical>self</radical> sits on top — that nose you point at when you mean you — and directly underneath it, your <radical>heart</radical>. Nose above, heart below, and running between the two of them all day long is the one thing you never have to decide to do. In through the nose, down to the heart, back out: <radical>breath</radical>.
k-breath.reading_mnemonic: Soku is the swimmer who comes up after far too long under and takes one enormous ragged gulp — 「<reading>そく</reading>」 — nose first, heart going like a hammer. That is what a breath you badly needed sounds like. そく.

k-daughter.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>woman</radical> at the left, and beside her the whole shape of <radical>stopping</radical>: the eye that has seen something and the foot that will not take another step. She is planted in the doorway with her arms folded, and the young one is not going out tonight. A girl who gets stopped at the door is somebody's <radical>daughter</radical>.
k-daughter.reading_mnemonic: Jou is how the neighbours refer to her, drawn out and a shade too formal — 「<reading>じょう</reading>」 — the sort of address you use for a girl of good family who is very definitely not allowed out. She hears じょう and rolls her eyes.

k-daytime.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>body</radical> is slumped across the top with a single <radical>drop</radical> of sweat coming off it, and directly underneath sits the <radical>sun</radical>, pinned against a flat line of <radical>ground</radical>. It is straight overhead and there is no shade left anywhere. Work has stopped and everyone has lain down. This is the flattening middle of the <radical>daytime</radical>.
k-daytime.reading_mnemonic: Chuu the loyal mouse will not nap through it. While every other body is flat out he stands at his post in the full sun, squeaking 「<reading>ちゅう</reading>」 on the hour so that nobody oversleeps. Absurdly devoted, ちゅう, right through the worst of it.

k-doctor.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>box on its side</radical>, its open mouth turned towards you, and lying inside it an <radical>arrow</radical> — the one they have just drawn out of you, dropped in the tray. The lid comes down over the arrowhead and the wound both. Whoever owns that box and knows what to do with what comes out of you is the <radical>doctor</radical>.
k-doctor.reading_mnemonic: Ii is the noise she makes while examining you: one short noncommittal 「<reading>い</reading>」 as she looks at the wound, and another as she drops the arrow into the tray. Nothing whatsoever about い tells you whether it is bad news.

k-end.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the <radical>tree</radical>: a <radical>stick</radical> straight up the middle, branches <radical>split</radical> away either side, and laid across the very top an extra <radical>lid</radical> of a stroke, drawn longer than the <radical>one</radical> below it. That top bar marks the last inch of the highest twig — as far up as this tree is ever going to go. The tip is the <radical>end</radical>.
k-end.reading_mnemonic: Matsu is the woodsman who only ever takes the tip. He climbs the whole tree, snips the last bud off the top of it, and calls down 「<reading>まつ</reading>」 to say he has got there. まつ means there is nothing above him.

k-evening.meaning_mnemonic: Three strokes and nothing else: a curve like the shoulder of a hill, with one line falling through it. It is the moon, only half up and not yet bright, caught at the exact moment the light goes flat and blue and everything loses its edges. Nothing has happened yet. The whole character is one picture of <radical>evening</radical> starting.
k-evening.reading_mnemonic: Seki comes out onto his step at this hour every night, and you hear him before you see him — that wet, rattling 「<reading>せき</reading>」 of a cough carrying right down the street. When せき starts up, the light has gone.

k-father.meaning_mnemonic: Two arms crossing over each other at the top, two legs braced wide underneath. It is a stance, not a face — the shape of a man standing square in a doorway with his arms folded, filling the whole frame, waiting to hear what you have got to say for yourself. Everybody recognises that silhouette: <radical>father</radical>.
k-father.reading_mnemonic: Fu is the long breath out through the nose that he gives you instead of an answer — 「<reading>ふ</reading>」 — arms still folded. Not angry. Not pleased either. Just ふ, and you will be hearing it for the rest of your life.

k-friend.meaning_mnemonic: One stroke <radical>slides</radical> down from the top left across a bar of <radical>ground</radical>, and underneath it a <radical>right hand</radical> comes up to meet it. Two hands reaching in from opposite directions and closing on each other. Nobody is being paid for this and nobody is in charge of anybody. That is a <radical>friend</radical>.
k-friend.reading_mnemonic: Yuu is the one who is always there before you, hand already out, drawing the greeting into a long two-beat call across the car park — 「<reading>ゆう</reading>」 — before you have even shut the car door. ゆう means somebody is glad to see you.

k-gone.meaning_mnemonic: A mound of <radical>earth</radical> on top, and underneath it that little sealed <radical>cocoon</radical>, tucked well out of sight. Whatever was inside wrapped itself up, went under the soil, and never came back out. You can dig the whole mound over and there is nothing left in there to find. It is <radical>gone</radical>.
k-gone.reading_mnemonic: Kyo is the magician who buries things and cannot get them back. He taps the mound, says 「<reading>きょ</reading>」 with a flourish, and that is genuinely the end of the trick. No reappearance, no second half. きょ, and it is gone.

k-he.meaning_mnemonic: A single <radical>step</radical> at the left edge, and beside it a hide being hauled off in one sheet — all <radical>skin</radical>, no animal left. Someone walked past carrying it a moment ago and is already down the road. You never saw the face, only the back of him. That man over there, the one you point at and cannot name: <radical>he</radical>.
k-he.reading_mnemonic: Hii is the little intake of breath you make when the man in the skin cloak goes past without a word — 「<reading>ひ</reading>」 — and by the time you have finished it he is round the corner. Every single time you catch sight of him: ひ.

k-heart.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>wide box</radical> of a room, and shoved right to the back of it a store of <radical>rice</radical> with something <radical>big</radical> planted on top of the pile. You have to walk through every other room in the house to reach it, and nobody outside the family ever does. The deepest room is the building's <radical>heart</radical>.
k-heart.reading_mnemonic: Ou is the grandmother who lives in that back room and has not come out in years. Knock and you get one long syllable through the paper door — 「<reading>おう</reading>」 — meaning she heard you and no, you may not come in. おう, from the very back of the house.

k-husband.meaning_mnemonic: Take the <radical>big</radical> figure — the <radical>person</radical> standing with both arms flung out wide — and lay one more bar across the top of it like a <radical>lid</radical>, so there are <radical>two</radical> horizontal strokes up there instead of one. That extra line is the pin through his topknot. He is grown, he is married, and he would like you to notice: <radical>husband</radical>.
k-husband.reading_mnemonic: Fu is the same breath out through the nose you learned from his father, inherited exactly — arms folded in the doorway, one 「<reading>ふ</reading>」, no further comment offered. Getting married did not change it in the slightest.

k-me.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> stands at the far left, and stacked up beside him is a <radical>big</radical> load: a <radical>sheep</radical> he has to carry in, then <radical>split</radical> into portions for everyone else before he takes any himself. He does the hauling and he eats last, and when he speaks he uses the humble word for <radical>me</radical>.
k-me.reading_mnemonic: Boku is the errand boy who answers every question about who did it with the same word: 「<reading>ぼく</reading>」. Broke the gate? ぼく. Carried the sheep up the hill? ぼく. He never says his own name, so ぼく is the only name you have for him.

k-mister.meaning_mnemonic: Someone has swept the whole yard with a <radical>broom</radical>, one stroke that <radical>slides</radical> away to the left, until the <radical>ground</radical> is spotless. Then he opens his <radical>mouth</radical> and gives out tomorrow's orders. He is not the emperor, only the man directly above you — the <radical>mister</radical> whose name gets attached to every younger man in the room.
k-mister.reading_mnemonic: Kun is the teacher who refuses to use first names. Every boy in the class gets the same syllable barked after his surname — 「<reading>くん</reading>」 — as the seating chart comes out. Tanaka-くん. Sato-くん. It is how you know he means you.

k-morning.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> is caught low in a <radical>cross</radical>-braced frame on the left, still climbing, while over on the right the <radical>moon</radical> has not gone down yet. Both of them are up there at once. That happens for about twenty minutes a day, and only ever at one end of it: <radical>morning</radical>.
k-morning.reading_mnemonic: Chou is the long-distance runner who is out before anybody else, and she stretches her greeting the whole length of the street as she passes your window — a long, unreasonably cheerful 「<reading>ちょう</reading>」. If you hear ちょう, the moon is still up.

k-mother.meaning_mnemonic: A figure kneeling with her arms wrapped round in front of her, and two dots marking the breasts that fed you. The entire character is built around those two points; take them out and it turns into a different word altogether. They are the reason the shape exists at all, and the reason you call her <radical>mother</radical>.
k-mother.reading_mnemonic: Bo is the one syllable a baby manages long before it manages anything else — 「<reading>ぼ</reading>」 — blown out with a bubble of spit and aimed straight at whoever is holding it. She answers to ぼ years before she answers to her own name.

k-night.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>lid</radical> is pulled across the top of the sky, and a <radical>person</radical> slips underneath it just as the last of the <radical>evening</radical> drains away. Once that lid is on, nothing more gets in — no sun, no colour, nobody else. The lid down over the evening, with somebody still out under it: <radical>night</radical>.
k-night.reading_mnemonic: Ya is the yakitori man who only opens once the lid is down. The cart comes out of nowhere, the lantern goes up, and he calls one syllable into the dark — 「<reading>や</reading>」 — which is the entire advertisement. If you can hear や, it is night.

k-nightfall.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> on the left has finally been let off: the shape on the right is the one that squeezes out from under the heavy lid and walks away <radical>exempt</radical>. Its shift is done, it has clocked out, and it drops below the roofline without waiting to be dismissed. The sun excused from duty is <radical>nightfall</radical>.
k-nightfall.reading_mnemonic: Ban is the night watchman who takes over the moment the sun clocks off. He drags the gate shut and announces himself to the empty street — 「<reading>ばん</reading>」 — one flat syllable, every night, so you know the day is closed.

k-on-foot.meaning_mnemonic: A single <radical>step</radical> at the left edge, and beside it the entire shape of a <radical>run</radical> — thigh forward, foot planting, ground coming loose behind. Except there is no horse here, no cart, and no road worth the name. Whatever is getting done today is getting done <radical>on foot</radical>.
k-on-foot.reading_mnemonic: Toto the door-to-door turtle has never once taken a ride. He carries the sample doors on his shell and walks the entire round, and he announces himself at every house with the same syllable before he knocks — 「<reading>と</reading>」. と, and another mile.

k-private.meaning_mnemonic: A stalk of <radical>grain</radical> leans over on the left, and tucked in behind it on the right is a little <radical>cocoon</radical>, sealed tight. Nobody else knows it is there. You grew the whole crop out in the open, then wrapped one seed away for yourself and told no one. Grain kept back inside a cocoon is what is <radical>private</radical>.
k-private.reading_mnemonic: Shi is the quiet one who keeps her own small field behind the house, and when anyone asks what she is growing in it she says 「<reading>し</reading>」 and closes the gate. Not rude, exactly. Whatever is in there is hers, and し is the only answer you are ever going to get.

k-second-1.meaning_mnemonic: A stalk of <radical>grain</radical> on the left, and beside it the <radical>small</radical> mark. Not the ear, not the stalk — one single bristle off the very top of the head, the thinnest thing on the entire plant. Slice up an hour the same way and the sliver you are left holding is one <radical>second</radical>.
k-second-1.reading_mnemonic: Byou is the hospital timekeeper with the stopwatch, and she counts out loud in a flat clipped bark — 「<reading>びょう</reading>」, びょう, びょう — one for every tick. She will not speed up and she will not stop. びょう is a single second landing.

k-submit.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> on the left, and on the right <radical>two</radical> bars stacked over a line of <radical>ground</radical>, carried on a <radical>stick</radical> each and <radical>split</radical> apart at the foot into a pair of legs. It is a tray on a stand, lifted with both hands. He is not setting it down — he is holding it up for somebody above him to take, which is what it is to <radical>submit</radical> a thing.
k-submit.reading_mnemonic: Kyou is the offering-bearer who never lowers the tray. He walks the entire length of the hall with it over his head, announcing himself at every pillar — 「<reading>きょう</reading>」 — until somebody finally takes the weight off him.

k-uncle.meaning_mnemonic: A stick of <radical>divination</radical> up in the corner, a <radical>small</radical> mark beside it, and a <radical>right hand</radical> reaching in underneath to scoop the pair of them up. This is the younger brother: not the head of the family, so he gets the fortune-telling twigs and the small share, and he turns up at New Year to read your future for a laugh. Your <radical>uncle</radical>.
k-uncle.reading_mnemonic: Shuku is that uncle, and he arrives every year with the same trick. He shuffles the sticks, throws them down, sucks his teeth, and pronounces 「<reading>しゅく</reading>」 as though it settles the matter. Nobody knows what しゅく means. He will not explain.

k-what.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> stands at the left with a line in his hand — you can see the <radical>barb</radical> at the end of it, and a flat bar of <radical>ground</radical> above the open <radical>mouth</radical> below. He has hooked something out of the water and hauled it up, and now he is just staring at it with his mouth hanging open, because he has no idea <radical>what</radical> it is.
k-what.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the fire-breathing crow drops onto the power line above him and looks at the thing on the hook. She has never seen one either. All she manages is one puzzled croak — 「<reading>か</reading>?」 — with a little puff of flame behind it. か? か? Neither of them knows.

k-who.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Words</radical> stand on the left, and on the right an <radical>old bird</radical> with its head cocked, waiting. You have been talking for ten minutes and the bird still cannot work out which person you mean. It hops in closer and asks the only question you have left it: <radical>who</radical>?
k-who.reading_mnemonic: Sui is the owl who works the gate. She leans down, blinks once, and hoots 「<reading>すい</reading>」, which in owl means name, please. Nobody gets past her without answering it. すい, すい, until you say who you are.

k-wife.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>woman</radical> at the bottom, and above her a <radical>broom</radical> held up on its <radical>stick</radical>, with a bar of <radical>ground</radical> ruled straight across the top. She is not sweeping out somebody else's household here. The broom, the floor and the roofline over both are hers, and the person who runs them is the <radical>wife</radical>.
k-wife.reading_mnemonic: Sai is the one who actually decides. Ask her husband anything and he glances sideways at her first; she gives one flat 「<reading>さい</reading>」 and that is the answer on behalf of both of them. さい settles it.

k-yesterday.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> on the left, and on the right a <radical>stick</radical> driven upright into the dirt with one stroke that <radical>slides</radical> off it. That stick is a sundial, and the shadow it threw is still scratched into the ground beside it. The sun has moved on. The mark it left behind belongs to <radical>yesterday</radical>.
k-yesterday.reading_mnemonic: Saku is the old gardener who checks his shadow-stick every dawn and then grumbles about how much better the light was 「<reading>さく</reading>」 — his one-word shorthand for the day before. Nothing is ever as good as さく was.

k-zero.meaning_mnemonic: <radical>Rain</radical> across the whole top of the character, and underneath it a <radical>person</radical> kneeling on the bare <radical>ground</radical> while the clerk presses her <radical>stamp</radical> down onto the ledger. It lands in the column where this year's crop should have been counted, and what it prints there is one perfect round <radical>zero</radical>. The rain took the lot.
k-zero.reading_mnemonic: Rei is that clerk. She is scrupulously polite about it — a small bow, a murmured 「<reading>れい</reading>」 — and then she inks the nothing into your row and moves down the line. れい, bow, zero. She has done it forty times today.

k-employee.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the whole character as a laminated badge clipped above a fat coin-purse, swinging on a lanyard. At the mountain trail's summit, a vending-machine gatekeeper won't sell a drink until that badge gets stamped and your name goes into the purse-shaped ledger — congratulations, you're now an employee of the mountain.
k-employee.reading_mnemonic: The gatekeeper is a retired innkeeper everyone calls <reading>Inn</reading>, and she grunts <reading>いん</reading> every time she stamps a badge — one grunt per hire, and by dusk her voice is gone from saying it all day.
k-employee.description: 員 rarely stands alone as a word for 'employee' — it is a suffix meaning roughly 'a person belonging to,' always riding on a job title, company, or club, closer to '-er' than to a stand-alone noun.

k-tooth.meaning_mnemonic: See the whole character as one wide gear-wheel rim, its edge cut into a ring of jagged points — as much a grinning mouthful of teeth as a machine part. At Grandma Kane's shrine, the temple cats keep gnawing the bell's toothed rim like a giant biscuit, filing their own teeth flat until the metal gleams like a jaw.
k-tooth.reading_mnemonic: One shrine cat, nicknamed <reading>Shii</reading> for the hiss she makes mid-gnaw, clamps onto the bell rim and hisses <reading>し</reading> through the gap where a tooth used to be.

k-body.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the whole character as a lean human outline with one rigid wooden post running straight down its spine, arms locked out to the sides. At Sei's school sports field, the club drags out this same stiff training dummy for every first-aid drill, and by the end of term everyone just calls it 'the body.'
k-body.reading_mnemonic: Someone always loops a spare <reading>tie</reading> around the training dummy's neck before drills, and the coach barks <reading>たい</reading> to snap the team to attention — same dummy, same crooked tie, every single practice.

k-thing.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the whole character as a lumpy, unlabeled shape — not quite a box, not quite a creature, just a mass with no clean outline. Koichi keeps a lost-and-found bin like this behind the konbini counter, crammed with a bent umbrella, half a slipper, and something sticky, and after six months he just labels the whole bin 'thing.'
k-thing.reading_mnemonic: Koichi holds up a single lost <reading>boot</reading> from the bin and grunts <reading>ぶつ</reading> — the general word for 'thing,' because after six unclaimed months, calling it a boot feels oddly specific.

k-meal.meaning_mnemonic: See the whole character as one plate: a heaping bowl of rice on the left, and crammed right against it, a second helping someone snuck onto the tray before anyone could stop them. Two portions jammed into one shape, because the character isn't just rice — it's the whole meal, second helpings included.
k-meal.reading_mnemonic: Han, the half-and-half chef, slices your whole dinner clean down the center before you can protest — that's just how he works here. You call out his name, <reading>Han</reading>, and he answers with a proud <reading>はん</reading>, holding up two identical plates like it settles the matter.

k-tea.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the whole character as a single steaming cup: delicate leaves curling up out of the top like steam made visible, sitting over a squat little cup shape below. That curling steam is the entire picture — the character doesn't need anything else to mean tea.
k-tea.reading_mnemonic: A dance instructor spins through the tearoom mid cha-cha lesson, a full teacup balanced on his palm, counting the beat out loud, <reading>ちゃ</reading>-<reading>cha</reading>-cha — right until the cup tips and the lesson ends the same soaked way every time.

k-hit.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the whole character as a dart frozen mid-flight: its little flight feathers up top, driven dead center into a square target below. One clean throw, no wobble, landing exactly where it was meant to — that's the whole shape, something hitting precisely on the mark.
k-hit.reading_mnemonic: The dart thrower celebrates his bullseye by kicking the target stand in triumph and instantly regrets it, hopping and hissing through his teeth: <reading>とう</reading>, my <reading>toe</reading>, my <reading>toe</reading>! Somehow he still lands the next throw dead center.

k-ill.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the whole character as a lean-to sickroom: a slanted roof propped against the wall, and underneath it a patient stretched flat, legs sticking straight out past the edge of a blanket too short to cover them. The whole shape is basically a tiny room built for exactly one thing — someone too ill to get up.
k-ill.reading_mnemonic: The former beauty-pageant queen lies flat under the sickroom's too-short blanket, moaning into her pillow, sure this is the least glamorous she has ever looked: <reading>びょう</reading>, she groans, sounding exactly like the first half of <reading>beauty</reading> gone hoarse.

k-section.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 部 as a squat metal filing cabinet chopped into stacked drawers, one per department. A clerk yanks open the wrong drawer, gets buried under someone else's forms, shoves them back, and slams shut the drawer marked for his own section.
k-section.reading_mnemonic: A moth called <reading>Bu</reading> gets shut inside that same drawer overnight and beats its wings against the forms, the frantic drumming going <reading>ぶ</reading>, <reading>ぶ</reading>, <reading>ぶ</reading>, until dawn finally opens the drawer and lets it stagger free.

k-pedestal.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 台 as a squat stone pedestal, wide and flat on top, sturdy legs planted underneath. Workers winch a bronze statue onto it inch by inch, and the block doesn't budge under the weight — solid, load-bearing, built for exactly this: holding something up.
k-pedestal.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Dai</reading>, the giant baby, climbs onto that same pedestal to pose like a statue. One stomp cracks the stone with a boom that rattles windows, and he wails <reading>だい</reading>, <reading>だい</reading> as the block crumbles beneath him.

k-courtyard.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 庭 as a private courtyard behind a house: raked white gravel, a crooked pine in one corner, and a stubborn goat that has moved in permanently, chewing through the ivy on the low wall. Nobody has managed to evict it from the family's own patch of outside — the courtyard.
k-courtyard.reading_mnemonic: The groundskeeper, named <reading>Tei</reading>, sprints after the goat squatting in the courtyard, tripping over the raked gravel and yelling <reading>てい</reading>, <reading>てい</reading> with every failed lunge, gravel spraying across the whole swept quiet.

k-turn.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 番 as a ticket dispenser bolted to a wall, spitting out numbered slips one at a time. Customers file into a line strictly by whichever number they're holding, and nobody moves an inch out of place — the pure order of taking your turn.
k-turn.reading_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a guard named <reading>Ban</reading> slams a wooden stamp onto the counter each time a new number is called, the crack echoing <reading>ばん</reading> through the shop as the line shuffles forward one turn at a time.

k-empty.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, a hiker jams every coin into the lone vending machine. The lever clunks, the tray spins, and rattles down to nothing — no can, no snack, just a hollow clang. He cups his hands to the glass: every row sits bare, and above him the sky stretches on just as empty.
k-empty.reading_mnemonic: Still stuck at the summit, the hiker slumps against the machine and lets out a long, pigeon-like <reading>coo</reading> up at the empty sky — <reading>くう</reading>, over and over, rising and hollow, until it's the only sound left on the whole mountain.

k-brush-stroke.meaning_mnemonic: In the school art room, a boy is told to paint one careful stroke inside the blank canvas frame. His hand shakes, the brush skids sideways, and one line becomes ten, looping corner to corner until the frame is smeared black. The teacher sighs and pins it up anyway — technically, it's a picture now, made of every stroke that got away from him.
k-brush-stroke.reading_mnemonic: Back in the art room, the teacher looks at the smeared frame and can only manage a flat, deflated <reading>gah</reading> — <reading>が</reading> — the sound of someone giving up on a critique before it starts. He staples a ribbon to it anyway and calls it finished.

k-reflect.meaning_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank, a fisherman sets his lantern on a flat rock at dusk. The still water throws its light straight back up, doubling the flame, doubling his own face staring down at it. He waves; the water waves back a half-second late, like a cheap projector catching up — everything reflected, delayed, right back at him.
k-reflect.reading_mnemonic: Startled by his own doubled face in the water, the fisherman yelps <reading>Ay</reading> — <reading>えい</reading> — and the river throws the sound straight back at him a beat later, flat and unbothered, same as it did with the light.

k-roof.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi's konbini springs a leak the night of the first typhoon. Rain drums through a hole in the ceiling onto the onigiri shelf, so Koichi hauls a tarp up top and lashes it down himself, muttering that a shop without one is just an expensive puddle. From then on, the neighborhood just calls the place "the roof" instead of its real name.
k-roof.reading_mnemonic: Weeks later, the tarp is still up, now painted with a crude little <reading>oak</reading> tree Koichi drew himself — <reading>おく</reading> — because customers kept asking what was holding the whole roof together. Nobody has the heart to tell him it's just tarp and string.

k-inst.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's shrine has quietly become an institution: the mossy steps now lead through a turnstile, past a cat in a visor checking permits at a glass window, under the enormous bell rehung as a service chime, into a maze of numbered waiting rooms. That towering, bureaucratic compound is the whole picture: an institution.
k-inst.reading_mnemonic: At the same window, the visor cat's ink stamp has half-dried, so every ticket comes out a pale <reading>いん</reading>. She grumbles it sounds like <reading>bean</reading> paste smeared thin, and refuses to fetch a new pad before the shrine's afternoon bell.

k-bureau.meaning_mnemonic: Behind the beeping till, Koichi has partitioned off a booth barely wider than the onigiri shelf and nailed a sign reading BUREAU: parcels, stamps, tax forms, three queues, all squeezed into a space meant for register rolls. Somehow every errand routes through that one cramped booth - a whole bureau folded into a konbini corner.
k-bureau.reading_mnemonic: Wedged into that same booth, a customer three forms deep chokes on chalky bureau dust drifting off the tax stacks, coughing out something between a wheeze and <reading>きょく</reading>. Koichi just nods, because everyone who reaches window three sounds exactly like they're trying to say <reading>choke</reading>.

k-convenience.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the steep mountain trail, a hiker rounds the last switchback and finds a vending machine, impossibly, and beside it a portable toilet stencilled CONVENIENCE. A badger barrels in as the first raindrop falls, grateful someone put a facility exactly where every tired leg needs one: pure convenience.
k-convenience.reading_mnemonic: The badger's slam sends the vending machine's change chute rattling out coins, and the hiker who planned to buy one - a guy named <reading>Ben</reading> - just stands there muttering <reading>べん</reading> under his breath, resigned to waiting outside in the rain for his turn.

k-building.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's school gym floods every spring, so the sports field committee just annexes the old mansion next door, knocks through a wall, and calls the echoing ballroom the new gymnasium. Trophies now line marble staircases, badminton nets hang from chandeliers, and the merger becomes one sprawling building: half school, half mansion.
k-building.reading_mnemonic: The gym teacher, thrilled with his new marble domain, has taken to calling himself the <reading>かん</reading> instead of coach - loosely, <reading>Khan</reading> - and blows his whistle from the top of the staircase every morning like a monarch addressing the badminton court below.

k-near.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 近 as <radical>a bent signpost arrow</radical> that gave up pointing anywhere far and curled all the way around to jab at your own boots. On the mountain trail, the vending machine you swore was another hour up turns out to be one switchback away: near.
k-near.reading_mnemonic: At that vending machine, the hiker's little brother — pure <reading>kin</reading>, tagging along everywhere — presses his face to the glass and chants the machine's name like a drumbeat: <reading>きん</reading>. He is always, always this close.

k-slow.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 遅 as <radical>a shoe with a snail's shell bolted to the heel</radical>. At Sei's school, the last runner on the sports field drags that shell across the track, one soggy footprint every ten seconds while the whole field stands there waiting: slow.
k-slow.reading_mnemonic: The class hamster, <reading>Chi</reading>, is let loose to race him and loses on purpose, wheezing one flat unimpressed <reading>ち</reading> at the finish line — same track, same shell-heavy heel dragging in dead last.

k-walk.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 歩 as <radical>one sandal print stamped twice, heel then toe</radical>, like a stencil dragged forward by itself. At the riverbank, that print walks itself across the stepping-stones, landing dead center of each rock all the way to the far bank: walk.
k-walk.reading_mnemonic: Halfway across, the fisherman watching from the bank lets out one delighted <reading>ho</reading> — <reading>ほ</reading> — every time the print lands without a splash, cheering each dry step home.

k-exertion.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 勉 as <radical>a sweatband wrung out mid-cram, soaking the textbook page underneath</radical>. In the fluorescent glare of Koichi's konbini, a student camped by the onigiri shelf pulls an all-nighter before finals, wringing the band out again and again, refusing to stop: exertion.
k-exertion.reading_mnemonic: The clerk ringing up onigiri all night, <reading>Ben</reading>, groans the same sympathetic <reading>べん</reading> every time the sweatband hits the counter, cheering the cramming on until the beeping till finally goes quiet.

k-paper.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a flat gray sheet dragged straight out of a river current, dripping and thin as a wet leaf, its edges ragged where the fibers refuse to line up. A woman presses it against a wooden frame in the shallows, and by the time the sun has dried it stiff, it lies flat, blank, and waiting: paper.
k-paper.reading_mnemonic: At the same riverbank, a heron picks through the drying pulp and hisses <reading>し</reading> every time the wet sheet slips under its feet, that flat <reading>sheesh</reading> sound of air escaping, the exact noise you make when you finally get the paper flat.

k-window.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the back wall of Koichi's konbini, solid and windowless, until someone punches a single square hole through the plaster at eye level. Light floods in, the onigiri shelf glows in it, and every customer's eyes go straight to the one bright square cut into the dark: a window.
k-window.reading_mnemonic: At the same konbini, a raccoon dog crashes straight through the new opening chasing a dropped onigiri, skids across the tile, and the clerk can only gasp <reading>そう</reading>, that flat English <reading>so</reading> of someone watching it happen with no better word for it.

k-true.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the water ladle at Grandma Kane's shrine, tipped all the way back and filled past its rim so the water pours over both sides at once, nobody skimmed it, nobody faked the offering thin. That same reckless, overfull ladle is what the kanji draws: nothing held back, nothing false. True.
k-true.reading_mnemonic: One of the shrine cats leaps for the ladle, misjudges the step, and slams its shin against the stone stand, yowling <reading>しん</reading>, the sound of the English word <reading>shin</reading>, before limping off, the truest reaction any cat has given all day.

k-cut.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the gym teacher's whistle at Sei's school, blown so hard and sudden that the long note doesn't fade, it just stops, sliced off mid-breath like a rope snapped taut and severed in one motion. That dead, clean stop is the whole idea drawn into one character: cut.
k-cut.reading_mnemonic: A stray dog dashes onto Sei's field mid-drill, and the whistle cuts dead again, <reading>せつ</reading>, that clipped English <reading>set</reading> the teacher barks before chasing it off, the severed note still hanging in the air where the sound should have continued.

k-wind.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker's poncho suddenly balloons into one huge sail, hood snapping sideways, while a moth trapped inside beats against the fabric hunting for an exit that isn't there. The whole poncho leans hard in one direction, cloth cracking like a whip. That swollen, straining shape is wind.
k-wind.reading_mnemonic: At the vending machine on the mountain trail, the hiker doubles over and breathes out one long <reading>ふう</reading> — the same winded <reading>phew</reading> you'd sigh after a gust knocks you sideways, air rushing out just like the air that knocked you there.

k-move.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a stacked crate of onigiri by the door suddenly lurches forward on its own, dragging across the floor as if some engine had kicked on deep inside it, wheels shrieking while everything on the shelves sways as it goes. That sudden lurch — something still becoming something moving — is move.
k-move.reading_mnemonic: Koichi lurches out of the way and yelps <reading>どう</reading> — a flat, startled <reading>doh</reading> — as the crate rumbles past the beeping till and rocks the onigiri shelf on its way through.

k-cool.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, the water freezes over so fast mid-current that a dragonfly gets sealed inside the ice, wings still spread, the current still visibly moving beneath its trapped silhouette. The whole surface holds that one frozen, glassy chill, water and insect both stopped cold in the same instant.
k-cool.reading_mnemonic: A swimmer named <reading>Ray</reading> wades into the river and the cold hits so fast he gasps <reading>れい</reading> — like shouting his own name — freezing mid-step right where the dragonfly sits trapped in the ice.

k-music.meaning_mnemonic: In the schoolyard at Sei's school, a lone tree is strung branch to branch with dozens of tiny bells, and a squirrel scrambling up through them sets off a cascade of ringing that spreads out through the echoing hallways, so rich and comforting that class doesn't even mind the interruption. That whole chiming, swaying tree is music.
k-music.reading_mnemonic: Sei gawks up at the tree, mouth open, murmuring <reading>がく</reading> — pure <reading>gawk</reading> — unable to look away from the bells still swinging long after the squirrel is gone.

k-transmit.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 伝 as a hunched courier crouched on Grandma Kane's mossy steps, passing a folded paper hand to hand without once looking up. Cats bat it along underfoot, step after step, until it lands under the enormous bell. The message has crossed the whole shrine untouched: transmit.
k-transmit.reading_mnemonic: At the bell, an eel called <reading>Denny</reading> lives coiled in the rope. Anyone who tugs the bell to ring it gets a jolt, yelping <reading>でん</reading> as the shock jumps up their arm. The courier's paper still gets through — Denny just likes his cut of the news.

k-question.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 問 as a gate with a mouth built into the crossbar, shouting through the bars at Sei's school. A latecomer rattles the locked school gate and the mouth in the gate shouts back louder than they did, demanding to know why they're late. Nobody outside gets in without answering the gate's question.
k-question.reading_mnemonic: Outside that same gate, Mon-Bun — the scholarly rabbit twins — bicker without pause, blaming each other for muddling the question. They let out one long identical <reading>moan</reading> that comes out as <reading>もん</reading>, echoing off the bars, and they're still moaning it when the gate creaks open.

k-trip.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 旅 as a tattered flag flapping at the head of the mountain trail, a whole line of hikers trudging after it up the steep slope. Nobody questions where the flag leads; they just follow, boots slipping on gravel, until the trail spits them out at the lone vending machine at the top. That whole staggering line is a trip.
k-trip.reading_mnemonic: Leading them is a llama guide named <reading>Rio</reading>, bleating <reading>りょ</reading> at every switchback to keep the line moving. By the vending machine he collapses first, legs folded, still muttering it between breaths.

k-attend.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 仕 as a clerk standing bolt upright behind Koichi's konbini till, spine straight as a blade, saluting every customer like a samurai posted at his station. He never sits, never slouches, just attends the register from open to close. That rigid stance at his post is the whole meaning: attend.
k-attend.reading_mnemonic: Beside him works a hedgehog cashier named <reading>Shea</reading>, who hisses <reading>し</reading> through her teeth every time the till beeps too loud. The clerk never breaks his salute, but Shea flinches at every beep, still hissing it under her breath at closing.

k-descend.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 降 as a steep staircase cut into a mountainside, a slope on the left and two hurried footprints stamped down the steps on the right. A crate tips off the vending machine at the top and thunders down every step, bottles bouncing all the way to the bottom. A hill with feet already halfway down it: descend.
k-descend.reading_mnemonic: Koichi treks up that same trail himself to restock the vending machine, and when the last case slips from his arms and crashes down every step behind him, he just sighs <reading>こう</reading> — more <reading>cough</reading> than word — and watches it disappear downhill.

k-transit.meaning_mnemonic: See 渡 as a river drawn in three dripping strokes beside a row of measured footprints stamped straight across the water, like someone counting out each step from one bank to the other. The current never covers the marks; they lead all the way to the far side. That is transit: crossing counted out, step by step.
k-transit.reading_mnemonic: Toto wades into the shallows with a sample door strapped to his shell, testing each stepping stone before he trusts it, and every plant of his foot lands with a flat <reading>と</reading>, like a knuckle rapping a <reading>door</reading>, all the way to the far bank.

k-dwell.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 住 as one tall lamp standing bolt upright beside a smaller upright post, both planted in the exact same square of ground for years, never leaning even in strong wind. Moss climbs the two of them at the same slow rate — something planted in one place so long it has stopped being separate from the place. dwell.
k-dwell.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one cat never wanders past the mossy steps — Jusuke, who has lived under the bell so long nobody remembers him arriving. Every time it tolls, he grumbles <reading>じゅう</reading>, low in his throat, like the word <reading>chew</reading> dragged out twice as long.

k-nothingness.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 無 as a school gym floor scorched flat by a stage fire the night before a show, every prop gone, only four faint threads of smoke still rising off the ash line where the curtain stood. Walk onto that floor and there is nothing left to trip on, nothing to see — just an empty rectangle. nothingness.
k-nothingness.reading_mnemonic: A stray cow named Muu wanders into that same burned-out gym through Sei's echoing hallway, nobody around to shoo her out. Her only sound bounces off the bare walls, a flat <reading>む</reading>, like a drawn-out <reading>moo</reading> nobody is there to hear.

k-first-time.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, you grab the frayed rope and swing the huge bell for the first time in your life. The clapper catches wrong, and instead of a clean toll it screeches like a rusty gate, sending every cat on the mossy steps bolting off at once. That flinching, unrepeatable racket is what a first time actually sounds like.
k-first-time.reading_mnemonic: Still ringing in your ears, the shrine's fattest cat gives one hoarse, botched yowl — not a full meow, just a wheezy <reading>しょ</reading>, like a magician trying to <reading>show</reading> off a trick that didn't land. Every disastrous first attempt at that bell gets remembered by that one broken sound.

k-department.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's school has exactly one door at the end of the main hallway, its hand-lettered plaque nailed on crooked, at an angle no carpenter would allow. Every subject in the building — science, math, home ec — funnels through that single lopsided doorway, because nobody built a second one. That one overloaded, off-kilter door is the department.
k-department.reading_mnemonic: Kaa perches on the power line above that crooked doorway and coughs a puny puff of flame that singes the plaque a shade darker each week. The cough comes out hoarse and flat, <reading>か</reading>, like a stalling <reading>car</reading> engine — the sound the school now associates with that overworked door.

k-utmost.meaning_mnemonic: At the very top of the mountain trail, past where the vending machine has any business being, one hiker drops face-first onto the last flat rock before the ground falls away. There's no path beyond it, no signpost, nothing — just the absolute edge of what the trail has to give. That collapsed, can't-go-further spot is the utmost.
k-utmost.reading_mnemonic: Flat on that last rock, the hiker lets out one long <reading>さい</reading>, a groan that trails off exactly like an exhausted <reading>sigh</reading>. Reaching the utmost point, it turns out, feels a lot less like victory and a lot more like collapsing.

k-topic.meaning_mnemonic: Above the school gate somebody has bolted one steel plaque so heavy it will never come down: a single carved word, and nothing else, because the sign only ever holds one thing at a time. Nobody argues about what today's topic is — it's the one word on the plaque, full stop, the whole gate looking up at it before the bell even rings.
k-topic.reading_mnemonic: Dai, the giant baby the size of a truck, crawls up to that same gate and still can't read the plaque. He throws his head back and wails his own name, <reading>Dai</reading>, at a pitch that registers as <reading>だい</reading> on every seismograph in town, and the plaque shudders on its bolts.

k-promise.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, two friends tie a rope between two posts and swear to meet on this exact spot every year — a promise, sealed with a knot. The current tugs the wet rope smaller and smaller each season, so the exact spot one of them insisted on is really only ever approximately where the knot has shrunk to by now.
k-promise.reading_mnemonic: A fisherman named <reading>Yaku</reading> checks that knot every morning, tugging it once and grunting <reading>やく</reading> in satisfaction when it holds, then again next year when it has shrunk another inch, grunting the same <reading>やく</reading>, promise apparently unbroken.

k-sound.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the steep mountain trail, the one improbable vending machine finally takes your coin and drops a can with a clang so loud it bounces off every rock on the way back down. That clang, ringing back at you from every side of the mountain at once, is the only sound for miles — which is exactly what your ear means by sound.
k-sound.reading_mnemonic: Every clang like that wakes something on the mountain: an echo spirit called <reading>On</reading>, who repeats the vending machine's ring straight back at you, moaning <reading>おん</reading> in the exact pitch of the can hitting the tray, over and over until the trail goes quiet.

k-whole.meaning_mnemonic: At closing time, Koichi stops itemizing the onigiri shelf. He sweeps every rice ball into one basket, rings it up as a single line, and the till beeps once for the whole lot — not some of the shelf, not most of it, the entire shelf, gone in one purchase.
k-whole.reading_mnemonic: The new cashier, <reading>Zen</reading>, doesn't do partial sales; he scans the whole basket in one motion and mutters <reading>ぜん</reading> under his breath every single night, like a chant for clearing the entire shelf in one go.

k-medicine.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, the back shelf holds unlabeled bottles nobody stocked, leaves poking from every cap and dripping bitter syrup onto the tiles. The night clerk swallows a capful anyway, grimacing, and his headache is gone before he reaches the till. That crooked, leafy, dripping shelf is exactly how the character is drawn: medicine.
k-medicine.reading_mnemonic: A <reading>Yak</reading> shoulders through the konbini door, snuffles the dripping medicine shelf, and swallows a whole bottle in one gulp. Its stomach gurgles, it throws its huge head back, and out comes a groaning <reading>やく</reading> loud enough to rattle the onigiri shelf.

k-revolve.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the character as a single cart wheel, drawn mid-spin, that has broken loose at the top of the mountain trail and gone rolling past the vending machine. It doesn't stop at the bend — it whips around, flips past the same rock it already passed once, and keeps going in one long dizzy loop down the slope: revolve.
k-revolve.reading_mnemonic: At the bottom of the trail the loose wheel clips the vending machine, and one stray coin spins out and won't lie flat, circling the gravel — a lone <reading>ten</reading>-yen piece. The hiker chases it, muttering <reading>てん</reading> each time it wobbles past again.

k-fall.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the character as a stone letting go of the riverbank edge, tumbling straight down through open air, and vanishing under the current without a splash big enough for anyone fishing nearby to notice. It's gone before it even hits bottom, weight simply giving way to gravity: fall.
k-fall.reading_mnemonic: Downstream, the fisherman who missed the splash finds the culprit lodged in the shallows: a plain grey <reading>rock</reading>. He nudges it loose with his boot, and it thunks back under the surface with a flat, hollow <reading>らく</reading>.

k-beforehand.meaning_mnemonic: Every morning before the shutters lift, a hook drops from the ceiling of Koichi's konbini and snags tomorrow's delivery truck through a hole in time, hauling in rice balls that haven't been made yet. The clerk restocks a full day early - whatever happens here has already happened first, beforehand.
k-beforehand.reading_mnemonic: The hook-wielder greeter, a lanky clerk everyone calls <reading>Yo</reading>, hollers <reading>よ</reading> every time a snagged delivery drops through the hole in time, one flat syllable for every rice ball that arrives a day too soon.

k-grade.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail a stonemason has chiseled the cliff into a staircase for decades, refusing anyone past the third stair without proof they've earned it. Each stair carries a number scratched into the rock, a rank you must be graded into before your foot may touch it.
k-grade.reading_mnemonic: The stonemason, a squat old man everyone on the trail calls <reading>Dan</reading>, stamps your hiking permit and grunts <reading>だん</reading> once for every stair he's decided you're worthy of, then turns his back before you can argue.

k-nickname.meaning_mnemonic: Every morning on Sei's school sports field, a rooster perched on the fence handles roll call instead of the teacher, and it refuses to crow anyone's assigned number. Instead it screeches out whatever nickname the class gave you last week, until the field rings with everyone's most embarrassing name at once.
k-nickname.reading_mnemonic: The rooster itself has a name - the groundskeeper calls it <reading>Go</reading> - and every crow comes out as one long <reading>ごう</reading>, stretched out over the whole field until the flag finally goes up and the actual class begins.

k-plank.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank a single wide plank has lain half in the water and half in the mud for as long as anyone remembers, warped by seasons of rain until it splits clean down the center with every storm. Villagers keep dragging the same cracked plank back to lay it flat, because it's still the only board wide enough to cross on.
k-plank.reading_mnemonic: Downstream at the same crossing, the chef <reading>Han</reading> - the one who serves every dish split exactly in half - squats over the cracked plank and slices his lunch on it, muttering <reading>はん</reading> with each cut, half for him and half for the current.

k-storey.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the character as a tall, narrow staircase carved straight into the mossy steps of Grandma Kane's shrine, each step drawn a little higher and greener than the last, climbing past the enormous bell toward a floor you can't yet see from the bottom. Every landing sits stacked on the one below it: storey.
k-storey.reading_mnemonic: A monk named <reading>Kai</reading> climbs the shrine steps every morning, counting each landing aloud so he doesn't lose track: <reading>かい</reading>, one floor, <reading>かい</reading>, another. The cats sunning themselves on the steps stop washing just to watch him pass.
k-storey.description: 階 rarely stands alone as the everyday word for a storey. In practice it almost always attaches to a number as the counter for building floors. きざはし is a rare, literary reading for a staircase; かい is the reading actually used day to day.

k-craft.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 工 as a squat steel I-beam — flat cap on top, flat foot on the bottom, one spine welded straight down the middle. A crew winches it upright on a bare lot and bolts it in before a single wall exists. That lone beam is the first thing raised on any job site: the shape of craft itself, construction standing on end.
k-craft.reading_mnemonic: Koichi wheels his restocking cart past the freshly bolted beam and clips his elbow on the corner. He lets out a flat <reading>coo</reading>, dragging the vowel out long like his till's slow beep: <reading>こう</reading>. Then he reroutes the onigiri delivery around it.

k-spot.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 点 as a hanko stamped too hard onto a test paper in the school's front hall. The seal bursts and four fat ink droplets spatter sideways across the score box. Each droplet dries into its own dark, unmistakable dot — a spot pressed into the page, a mark nobody can argue with.
k-spot.reading_mnemonic: The hall monitor everyone just calls <reading>Ten</reading> finds the spattered test on the floor and holds up all ten fingers, hissing <reading>てん</reading> like he's counting the ink spots one by one before confiscating the paper.

k-meadow.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 原 as a slab of white rock jutting low over the mountain trail, a thin spring bleeding out from underneath it, unstoppable, spreading downhill until the ground finally opens into a flat meadow of undisturbed grass. This is where the trail's only water starts — the meadow, the original spot everything downstream traces back to.
k-meadow.reading_mnemonic: A hiker named <reading>Gen</reading> kneels at the spring to refill her bottle, and the cold hits her wrist so hard she yelps <reading>げん</reading>, sharp enough that the grasshoppers in the meadow scatter for cover.

k-lady.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 婦 as a woman named Fumi sweeping Grandma Kane's mossy shrine steps at dawn in a long apron, her broom scraping stone in the same rhythm every morning while the shrine cats scatter out of her path. She works the steps top to bottom without once looking up — the picture of a lady running her own household, corner by corner.
k-lady.reading_mnemonic: At the shrine gate, Fumi leans her broom against the rail and blows out a long <reading>phew</reading>, a breathy <reading>ふ</reading> that scatters the incense smoke, before picking the broom back up to finish the steps.

k-idea.meaning_mnemonic: In a hallway at Sei's school, picture the whole kanji as one image: a heavy iron lid clamped over a beating heart, muffling every thump. Pressure builds until the lid cracks a finger's width open, and a single bright spark hisses free through the gap — that spark, still hot, is the idea.
k-idea.reading_mnemonic: That escaped spark turns out to be Eeko, a firefly who only ever says one sound. She loops once around the lockers and lets out a bright <reading>い</reading> — an <reading>eek</reading>-thin squeak of light — before ducking back through the crack in the lid to cool off.

k-change.meaning_mnemonic: In the fluorescent glare of Koichi's konbini, a customer catches his own reflection in the till's dark screen: upright on the left, but on the right the same body has folded double and sprouted a stubby tail. He watches, frozen, as one shape slides into the other, mid-blink — change.
k-change.reading_mnemonic: Outside the window, Kaa the fire-breathing crow has been watching the whole trick from the power line. He can't hold it in — he lets out a hoarse <reading>か</reading>, the same rasp as his name, <reading>Kaa</reading>, and a puff of flame scorches the wire above the sliding doors.

k-sentence.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, the temple cat has fallen asleep spread-eagle across the mossy steps, arms flung wide and legs crossed at the ankle. Afternoon light slats through the eaves and lands across her fur in neat, deliberate lines, stroke after stroke, until her whole back reads as one finished sentence.
k-sentence.reading_mnemonic: Mon-Bun, the rabbit twins, lean over the cat arguing about how it ends. One twin insists it needs a flourish on top, like a bread <reading>bun</reading>, and keeps hollering <reading>ぶん</reading> until the enormous bell rings and the cat twitches the whole sentence into a blur.

k-method.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, the water doesn't get to wander. Picture the whole kanji as a stone flume bolted into the bank, forcing every drop of the river through one narrow channel, in the same order, with no shortcuts and no exceptions — that fixed channel, followed exactly, is the method.
k-method.reading_mnemonic: Hou, an owl who lives on the flume post, keeps watch for cheaters. Whenever a drop tries to leap the channel early, he swivels his head and hoots <reading>ほう</reading> — a low <reading>whoa</reading> that echoes off the water — until the drop falls back into line.

k-generation.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, three fence posts lean out of the moss at different heights. A groundskeeper strings one rope low for the toddlers, one higher for the parents, one higher still for the grandparents, refusing to leave until all three cross the same posts. The tangle reads as one family: three generations roped to the same ground.
k-generation.reading_mnemonic: Sei, hand up before anyone asks, elbows in to fix the groundskeeper's ropes and gets both ankles lassoed for it. She yanks free, smooths her uniform, and announces the fix in one clipped syllable that sounds exactly like you'd <reading>say</reading> it: <reading>せい</reading>.

k-world.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, past the improbable vending machine, the ground drops away and the valley opens below: field after field, boxed by its own low fence, patchworked to the horizon without a gap. It isn't one field anymore, it's every field at once, hemmed edge to edge, the boundaries adding up to the whole world.
k-world.reading_mnemonic: The hiker who dragged you up here, whom you've taken to calling <reading>Kai</reading> for the noise he makes at every switchback, doubles over at the summit and lets out one long <reading>かい</reading> of relief before he even looks at the view.

k-politics.meaning_mnemonic: On the sports field at Sei's school, the flagpole has bent sideways overnight. Sei drags it upright, braces it with her shoe, and raps it flat-handed with a pointer each time it slumps, until the whole field stands at attention around one stick beaten perfectly straight. That correcting by force is politics: government as the art of straightening what keeps slumping.
k-politics.reading_mnemonic: Sei doesn't stop at the flagpole. She marches the whole class into rows and claps them straight, and every clap lands on the same syllable, sharp as a ruler on a desk: <reading>せい</reading>, which you'd spell in English the way you'd <reading>say</reading> a drill sergeant's count.

k-reign.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, the current thrashes every direction, slapping washing out of people's hands. Someone stacks flat stones into a low wall across the narrows, and the water that fought everyone all morning collects behind it into one flat, silent pool, obeying the wall completely. That taming of the flood is what this character means: to reign, to calm down.
k-reign.reading_mnemonic: The stone-stacker, a quiet type the other kids call <reading>Ji</reading> because he never says more than one syllable, watches his pool go still and finally speaks: <reading>じ</reading>, and nothing else, satisfied.

k-sex.meaning_mnemonic: 性 shows up as one stamped box on a school health form: the box for your inborn nature, whatever you were born as. Sei, always first to raise his hand, isn't satisfied checking it once — he stamps it three times and asks the nurse to grade his nature like an exam. Stamped and graded: that is your sex, your gender, your nature.
k-sex.reading_mnemonic: The nurse, exhausted, waves the form away and tells him to just <reading>say</reading> his name and leave — Sei straightens up and corrects her anyway: it's <reading>せい</reading>, properly stamped, thank you.

k-inter.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank the water sits mirror-still: a hiker leans over and his reflection leans back at the same angle, matching every twitch. He waves, the water waves back; he frowns, it frowns back — two sides doing the same thing to each other, neither one first. That two-way mirroring is 相: inter-, mutual, together.
k-inter.reading_mnemonic: The hiker, Sou, leans in close and mutters <reading>そう</reading> to his own reflection, daring it to answer — and right on cue, impossibly, the water mutters <reading>so</reading> straight back at him, word for word, syllable for syllable.

k-guest.meaning_mnemonic: The vending machine atop the mountain trail is the only comfort after that whole steep climb, and a hiker treats it like a hotel lobby: he drops his pack, kicks off his boots, and waits for someone to bring him tea. Mountain or not, he has appointed himself the honored guest, expecting service and a seat — 客: guest, visitor, customer.
k-guest.reading_mnemonic: His ride up was a foul-tempered <reading>yak</reading> that refuses to leave the summit now, planting itself by the machine like it's checked into a hotel — a guide radios down that a <reading>きゃく</reading> has arrived and shows no sign of ever checking out.

k-public.meaning_mnemonic: Koichi never locks the konbini doors — day, night, holiday, no difference — because in his head the shop stopped being his years ago and became everyone's. He restocks the onigiri shelf for total strangers like a prince tending his domain, open to anyone who walks in. That is 公: public, official, everyone's business.
k-public.reading_mnemonic: Regulars don't bother with his whole name anymore — they just call out the long stretched <reading>Ko</reading> of 'Koichi' as he blurs past restocking, and it comes out as one clipped <reading>こう</reading>, because efficiency belongs to the public queue, not to small talk.

k-profit.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 利 as one tool: a thin blade lying flat beside a heavy stalk of grain, both leaning the same way, like a scale about to tip. At Koichi's konbini the clerk nicks a rice sack's string with that blade, and the sack weighs heavier after the cut than before. The register just prints profit.
k-profit.reading_mnemonic: At the same konbini scale, the clerk keeps a dry <reading>reed</reading> tucked behind his ear for luck, and every time a sack outweighs itself he snaps the reed and grins, muttering a stretched <reading>り</reading> like he just got away with something.

k-task.meaning_mnemonic: See 務 as one overloaded figure: a spear on one shoulder, a stick raised in a striking hand, and one arm flexed hard under the weight — three demands crammed onto a single body, none optional. On the mountain trail the guide carries all three past every switchback, only dropping his shoulders at the vending machine on top. The task is done.
k-task.reading_mnemonic: A cow that wandered up years ago still blocks the trail near that vending machine until every task is read aloud to her. She answers each one with a flat <reading>moo</reading>, and that same flat sound is the reading <reading>む</reading> — one syllable, no complaints, task acknowledged.

k-transport.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 輸 as one vehicle: a wagon's two wheels bolted onto a hollowed dugout boat's hull, rolling the riverbank path and floating once the bank drops away. Crates get loaded on and it shoves off — wheels spinning uselessly underwater, hull scraping stone on land — yet the ugly thing drags everything across. That is transport.
k-transport.reading_mnemonic: The ferryman poling this contraption never learns anyone's name, so he calls every passenger the same drawn-out word as the wheels hit water: a long <reading>you</reading>. That same stretched syllable is the reading <reading>ゆ</reading>, hollered once as the crates lurch forward and the hull scrapes off from the bank.

k-status.meaning_mnemonic: See 格 as one gnarled tree at Grandma Kane's shrine, where each branch forks off at its own height and stops there, holding exactly one cat and no other — the top branch for the biggest cat, the lowest for the newest arrival. No cat may sit on a branch that isn't hers. That fixed, branch-by-branch order is status.
k-status.reading_mnemonic: Every visitor who climbs the shrine's mossy steps and sees the cats ranked branch by branch just stops and <reading>gawks</reading>, throat catching on the same flat sound as the reading <reading>かく</reading>. The shrine's one enormous bell seems to echo it back once for every branch in the tree.

k-gate.meaning_mnemonic: Picture two matching wooden panels, hinged and identical, standing across from each other at Grandma Kane's shrine, flanking the mossy steps. A cat darts between them and both panels swing shut at once, clapping together with a boom that sets the enormous bell ringing. Twin doors that only work as a pair — that's a gate.
k-gate.reading_mnemonic: Mon-Bun, the scholarly rabbit twins, argue at Grandma Kane's shrine, each ending every sentence with a flat <reading>もん</reading> — book-nerd slang for obviously. They stand together like the gate's own twin panels, and every <reading>Mon</reading> makes the enormous bell shiver on its hook.

k-turn-into.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, one battered vending machine waits by the summit sign. A hiker feeds it a coin, and instead of a drink, the whole machine shudders, its panels folding and reforming until it isn't a vending machine anymore — it's a wooden bench, still warm. That's turn into: one thing reshaping into another.
k-turn-into.reading_mnemonic: Sei reaches the summit first, hand up before anyone can ask, and plants herself by the vending machine that just turned into a bench. She declares it like a quiz answer: a crisp, smug <reading>せい</reading>, and hikers who arrive late swear they can still hear that <reading>say</reading> echo off the rocks.

k-sort-of.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer holds up an onigiri with the label torn clean off and asks what's inside. The clerk squints at it, sniffs it once, then waves a hand vaguely at the whole shelf — sort of like those, probably that kind of thing. Nobody presses further; sort of thing turns out to be a real answer here.
k-sort-of.reading_mnemonic: The clerk, whom regulars just call <reading>Zen</reading> for his permanent shrug, mutters a flat <reading>ぜん</reading> every time someone asks for specifics, sliding the mystery onigiri back onto the shelf without another word. Say his name fast enough and it collapses into the same flat <reading>ぜん</reading> — shrug included.

k-mask.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, something pale and square drifts down with the current — a blank wooden mask, one oval outline, two carved eye-holes. Someone wades in, fishes it out, and holds it right over their own face. Their expression vanishes, replaced by the mask's flat stare. That's a mask — a face swapped for a face.
k-mask.reading_mnemonic: The fisherman who drags it from the water, everyone calls him <reading>Men</reading> for the grunt he gives instead of talking, holds the mask to the sky and lets out a low <reading>めん</reading> like a verdict. From then on, every mask pulled from that river gets the same flat <reading>めん</reading> before anyone's allowed to touch it.

k-demolition.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a fat cat leaps onto the bell rope just to swing on it. The rope snaps, the enormous bell tears free, and it thunders down the mossy steps, cracking three of them to rubble. Grandma Kane just sighs — another Tuesday of demolition.
k-demolition.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane's apprentice, a boy named <reading>Kai</reading>, surveys the wreckage and sighs the count out loud: <reading>かい</reading> — the third bell disaster this year alone. He says it flat, already reaching for the broom.

k-bring-up.meaning_mnemonic: On Sei's sports field, the groundskeeper plants one droopy sunflower seedling in an old milk carton and waters it every recess. By the third week it has shot up past the goalposts, leaves like small hands reaching for the sky — proof of raising something up.
k-bring-up.reading_mnemonic: A tiny kid named <reading>Iku</reading> waters the sunflower every morning before the bell, chanting <reading>いく</reading>, いく, grow already — as if the word itself could drag the stalk taller.

k-drought.meaning_mnemonic: The riverbank that should be rushing with water is nothing but a maze of cracked, sun-baked mud plates. A heron stands in the middle on one leg, unable to remember what wet ground even felt like — the whole bank has gone bone dry, a total drought.
k-drought.reading_mnemonic: The same heron kicks an empty tin <reading>can</reading> across the cracked mud out of pure boredom. It rolls to a stop with a hollow <reading>かん</reading> — the only sound this drought-cracked riverbank makes all summer.

k-get-wet.meaning_mnemonic: A customer bursts through the door of Koichi's konbini soaked from collar to shoe, rain sheeting off him in one long trail across the tile straight to the onigiri shelf. He leaves a puddle so deep the beeping till stutters and dies — everything about him has gotten wet.
k-get-wet.reading_mnemonic: Koichi mops the puddle and mutters <reading>じゅ</reading>, じゅ, like he's wringing the sound out of a sponge — it comes out exactly like the first syllable of <reading>juice</reading>, which is unfortunately also what the floor now smells like.
k-get-wet.description: This character mostly means plain physical wetness — rain, tears, sweat. The "make love" sense is idiomatic, from a fixed phrase for an intimate scene in film or drama. On its own as a verb, it almost always just means damp, not romance.

k-correct.meaning_mnemonic: On the school sports field, the coach chalks one line across the track and rules that only a toe planted exactly on it counts. Every runner skids past it or stops short — except Sei, uniform still spotless, who lands a toe dead on the line without even trying, smug before the whistle even blows: correct.
k-correct.reading_mnemonic: Back in the classroom, the teacher asks who stopped exactly on the line. Sei's hand shoots up before she finishes asking, and he answers with his own name like it settles it: <reading>Sei</reading>, <reading>せい</reading> — crisp, correct, a little too pleased with himself.

k-straightaway.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, everything bends — the reeds, the ripples, the rope holding the ferry to its post. Only the ferryman's eye stays fixed dead ahead on the far bank. He refuses to glance down at the crooked water and poles straightaway across, blunt and honest about exactly where he's going: straight, no detour.
k-straightaway.reading_mnemonic: On the far bank, kids call the ferryman Chalky, because his pole is an actual stick of chalk that drags one straight white line across the water on every crossing. Ask him why and he barks the same flat answer every time: <reading>ちょく</reading>, <reading>chalk</reading> — straight, immediate, no explanation given.

k-suffering.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini, a customer grabs the last onigiri off the shelf by the door and bites in before checking the date. It's turned — bitter, warm, wrong — and his whole face folds in on itself right there under the fluorescent lights, the till beeping behind him like it's keeping score of his suffering.
k-suffering.reading_mnemonic: He doesn't groan, exactly — what comes out is a strangled little <reading>coo</reading>, like a dove that swallowed a coin. The cashier doesn't even look up. She's heard that same <reading>く</reading> from every unlucky customer who trusted that shelf after dark.

k-even.meaning_mnemonic: The mountain trail climbs brutal and uneven for an hour, every step steeper than the last, until it just stops — the ground opens into one perfectly flat clearing around the vending machine at the top, level in every direction, not a single rock out of place. After all that chaos, it's suddenly, completely even.
k-even.reading_mnemonic: A hiker drags himself into the clearing, drops his pack, and lets out one long <reading>hey</reading> — half greeting to the vending machine, half sigh at finally standing on ground that doesn't fight back. That flat exhale is exactly the sound of <reading>へい</reading>: level, calm, done.

k-clear-up.meaning_mnemonic: Rain floods the school's sports field mid-relay, runners skidding through mud while the crowd groans under dripping umbrellas. Then the clouds simply tear apart overhead, one shaft of sun lands square on the finish line, steam lifts off the soaked track, and the whole field is suddenly, brightly clear up.
k-clear-up.reading_mnemonic: As the sky clears, Sei's hand shoots up first as always, uniform spotless despite the mud, and she announces it to the whole field, loud and smug: <reading>せい</reading> — like she's the one who <reading>said</reading> the sky would clear.

k-heat.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the microwave runs three full cycles on one forgotten onigiri, the wrapper bubbling and warping, the till beeping in panic behind the counter. When the door finally pops open, a wall of heat rolls out thick enough to fog the whole drink case. Heat, plain and total.
k-heat.reading_mnemonic: The clerk mopping her forehead at the register is nicknamed <reading>Netsu</reading> for it, and every time that wall of heat rolls out she groans the sound of her own name, <reading>ねつ</reading>, dragging it out like she's wading through hot fishing nets.

k-negative.meaning_mnemonic: A stiff figure plants itself at the top of Grandma Kane's mossy steps, arms flung straight out, ankles crossed tight, blocking the path to the enormous bell. Cats stream around its legs but it will not move, will not ring, will not budge — every request meets the same flat refusal. Negative.
k-negative.reading_mnemonic: The shrine cat everyone calls <reading>Fu</reading>, curled against the stubborn figure's crossed feet, doesn't hiss so much as sigh through her nose — a flat little <reading>ふ</reading> of a breath, unimpressed by every visitor who tries to squeeze past.
k-negative.description: This kanji almost never stands alone in real sentences; you meet it glued to the front of other words as a flat negation prefix, closer to un- or non- in English than a standalone word for bad.

k-precipitous.meaning_mnemonic: The mountain trail narrows to a knife-edge ridge, the path pinching to nothing between two sheer drops, one wrong step from the vending machine improbably waiting at the top. No one has ever reached it and no one ever will — the position is precipitous, impregnable, sealed off from the world.
k-precipitous.reading_mnemonic: Guarding that narrow ledge is <reading>Ken</reading>, the shiba who never leaves his wall of antique swords, and every hiker who eyes the vending machine past him gets one warning bark of <reading>けん</reading> before he bares a blade in his teeth.
k-precipitous.description: Beyond the literal steep-cliff picture, this kanji usually carries a broader sense of danger or risk in real vocabulary — insurance, adventure, hazard — rather than physical steepness itself.

k-seethe.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the hot water tap for cup noodles sticks wide open. The broth climbs past the rim in fat white bubbles, hissing and multiplying until foam rolls off the counter and drips past the onigiri shelf. The clerk just watches it seethe, boil, and go faintly sour under the fluorescent lights.
k-seethe.reading_mnemonic: A jumpy regular named <reading>Futz</reading> keeps mashing the button, muttering <reading>ふつ</reading>, ふつ under his breath every time the noodle water surges past the rim. Say his nervous little ふつ ふつ and the reading is stuck in your head with the foam.

k-burn.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine a cat leaps onto the offering shelf and topples a candle into a bundle of incense sticks. They catch one by one, each tip glowing orange, until the whole bundle flares into a blaze crackling under the enormous bell before anyone notices the smoke.
k-burn.reading_mnemonic: The neighborhood kids call Grandma Kane <reading>Nan</reading>, and when the incense flares she comes flying out stamping sparks off the mossy steps, yelling the cat's name so fast it comes out <reading>ねん</reading>. Picture Nan hollering ねん at that cat, and the reading burns itself in.

k-current.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank a sandal slips off the washing stones and the current takes it instantly, spinning it past the reeds and around the bend before anyone can wade in. Nothing dropped here stays put; the whole river is one long current pulling everything the same direction, gone before you can call after it.
k-current.reading_mnemonic: A boy named <reading>Ryu</reading> wades out too far and the current takes him too, his voice trailing off in a long <reading>りゅう</reading>, りゅう as he's carried past the reeds and around the bend, already too far off to reach. Say Ryu's fading りゅう and you have the reading.

k-times.meaning_mnemonic: From above, Sei's running track looks like one square course boxed inside a bigger square fence, the same loop traced again and again by whoever's running it. Each full lap around that boxed-in course is one more time, and the count just keeps climbing while the loop never changes shape.
k-times.reading_mnemonic: Sei's PE teacher, a man everyone calls <reading>Kai</reading>, stands at the gate barking a number each time a runner completes the loop: <reading>かい</reading>, かい, かい, one shout per lap. By the tenth lap nobody's counting anything but Kai's voice landing on かい.

k-surpass.meaning_mnemonic: The mountain trail switches back for an hour, calves burning, every ridge a good place to quit. Then a vending machine appears, glowing at the very top, absurdly out of place. You ignore every sane stopping point and just keep going, legs shaking, until you surpass the last ridge and reach it.
